forsake

/for-SAYK/ - rhymes with make · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Forsake means to give up or renounce something one is attached to.

Offered a larger parish in the capital, the young priest chose not to forsake the mountain village that had raised him.

Example

Grandfather forsook chess after Grandmother died; the board stayed set in the parlor, mid-game, for eleven years.

Forsake is heavier than quit or drop because it names giving up something loved — the word carries the ache of the parting, which is why the untouched board says more than any announcement could.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

desert: Desert means to walk out on someone or something that counts on you — a post, a family, a crew — and it points hard at the betrayal. Forsake points at the attachment instead: what is forsaken was loved, and the word carries the ache of the parting.

relinquish: Relinquish means to give something up — a claim, a seat, control — usually formally and often under pressure; it is the word of contracts and committees. Forsake is the word of the heart: it wants an object someone loves, and the parting is felt as grief.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

treasure: hold something dear and keep it close

uphold: stand by a promise or duty when it is tested

Where it sits · how much the leaving costs the heart

drop → abandon → forsake

drop vs. forsake: Drop is far milder than forsake — you drop a hobby the way you drop a habit, and nobody mourns; to forsake is to give up something loved, and the loss aches.

abandon vs. forsake: Abandon is milder than forsake even so: you can abandon a broken umbrella without a flicker, while forsake carries the ache of leaving something loved.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — for-: completely, away (Old English)

Root — sake: to contend, to deny (Old English sacan)

Put it together: For- (completely, away — an Old English prefix, not the preposition) + sake (from Old English sacan, to contend or deny) = to deny something away entirely, to refuse it once and for all. The old verb sacan died out of English, so the pieces no longer build anything new — but its noun fossilized in the phrase 'for the sake of,' where sake once meant a cause worth contending for.

Why there's no relative to spot: The Old English verb sacan, 'to contend or deny,' survives nowhere in modern English as a living root — its only trace is the frozen noun in 'for the sake of.' So forsake has no family of look-alike cousins to lean on; the word must simply be learned whole, prefix and fossil together.

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / emotional

Forsake is literary and weighted: it wants an object someone loves or owes loyalty to — a home, a craft, an old friend, a faith. Abandon, this unit's plainer reference word, covers everything from umbrellas to buildings without a tremor; abjure, taught in this unit, renounces formally and in public. If nobody would grieve the parting, forsake is the wrong word.
